images.purpose: Visualises the erratic, random path characteristic of Brownian motion, giving students a concrete picture of what the observed 'jittery' movement actually looks like.

subject: Physics
title: Diffusion
description: The net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, resulting from their random motion.
learning_objectives: Define diffusion
Explain diffusion in terms of the random motion of particles
Describe factors that affect the rate of diffusion
explanation: Diffusion is the net movement of particles of a substance from a region where they are more concentrated to a region where they are less concentrated, continuing until the particles become evenly spread throughout the available space (a state of equilibrium concentration). Diffusion occurs because particles are in constant, random motion (as described by particle theory); even though each individual particle moves in a completely random direction at any given moment, the overall statistical effect of a very large number of particles moving randomly is a net drift from more crowded regions toward less crowded regions, simply because there are, on average, more particles available in the crowded region to randomly wander outward than there are particles in the less crowded region to randomly wander back in. Diffusion occurs readily in gases and liquids, where particles are free to move throughout the available space, but does not occur in solids under normal conditions, since particles there are held in fixed positions. The rate of diffusion is affected by factors including temperature (higher temperature increases particle speed, and therefore the rate of diffusion), the concentration difference (a greater difference produces faster net diffusion), and the mass of the diffusing particles (lighter particles generally diffuse faster than heavier ones, at the same temperature).
key_concepts: Net movement from high to low concentration
Occurs due to random particle motion (statistical effect over many particles)
Occurs in gases and liquids; not in solids under normal conditions

definitions.definition: The net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, resulting from their random motion, until concentration is even.

worked_examples.problem: A drop of ink is placed into a still glass of water. Explain, in terms of particle motion, why the ink gradually spreads throughout the water over time.
steps: Immediately after being added, the ink particles are highly concentrated in one small region of the water, with very few (if any) ink particles present elsewhere.
Both the ink and water particles are in constant, random motion.

Because there are initially many more ink particles in the concentrated region than elsewhere, more ink particles randomly wander out of this region (into the surrounding, less concentrated water) than water particles randomly wander into it carrying ink.

Over time, this net, random drift of ink particles outward, away from their initial high-concentration region, causes the ink to spread out and eventually become evenly distributed throughout the water.
worked_examples.answer: The ink diffuses because its particles, moving randomly, statistically tend to spread out from their initially crowded region toward the surrounding water, where they were less concentrated, until they become evenly distributed.

practical_applications: Gas exchange in the lungs, relying on diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide across membranes
Food preservation and flavouring processes, involving diffusion of substances such as salt or smoke
Industrial processes involving mixing, dissolving, and separating substances
common_mistakes: Describing diffusion as particles deliberately or purposefully moving toward lower concentration, rather than as a statistical, random-motion effect
Assuming diffusion occurs in solids in the same way as in liquids and gases
misconceptions: That individual particles somehow 'know' to move toward regions of lower concentration — each individual particle moves in a completely random direction at all times; it is only the large-scale, statistical effect of enormous numbers of randomly moving particles, combined with an initial concentration difference, that produces the observed net movement from high to low concentration, not any deliberate or directed motion of individual particles.
tips: Remember diffusion is a NET (overall, statistical) effect resulting from random individual particle motion, not the deliberate, directed movement of any single particle.

basic: State the direction of net particle movement during diffusion, in terms of concentration.
intermediate: Explain why diffusion occurs faster at a higher temperature.
advanced: Explain why diffusion does not occur, under normal conditions, in a solid.

exam_questions: Explain, using the concept of random particle motion, why perfume released in one part of a room eventually spreads to fill the entire room.

basic: From a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.
intermediate: A higher temperature gives particles greater average kinetic energy, causing them to move faster; faster-moving particles cover distance more quickly and undergo more frequent random collisions and movements, increasing the overall rate at which the net diffusion of particles from high to low concentration occurs.
advanced: In a solid, particles are held in fixed positions by strong intermolecular forces and are only able to vibrate in place, rather than moving freely from one location to another; without this free, large-scale movement of particles throughout the material, there can be no net drift of particles from a region of high concentration to a region of low concentration, so diffusion does not occur in a solid under normal conditions.
exam: The perfume particles are in constant, random motion; since they are initially highly concentrated at their point of release, and there is initially a much lower concentration of perfume particles elsewhere in the room, more perfume particles randomly wander away from the release point (into the rest of the room) than particles randomly wander back in from the rest of the room; this net, statistical drift, resulting purely from the random motion of a very large number of particles, gradually spreads the perfume throughout the entire room until it becomes evenly distributed.

summary: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to lower concentration, arising from the random motion of a large number of particles rather than any directed individual movement. It occurs in gases and liquids, and its rate increases with temperature and concentration difference.
revision_notes: Net movement: high concentration -> low concentration
Due to random motion (statistical effect over many particles)
Occurs in gases/liquids, not solids; faster at higher temperature

subject: Physics
title: Intermolecular Forces
description: The attractive and repulsive forces acting between the particles (atoms or molecules) of a substance, determining many of its physical properties.
learning_objectives: Describe intermolecular forces as forces acting between particles
Explain how the strength of intermolecular forces relates to the state of matter of a substance
Relate intermolecular forces to melting point, boiling point, and other physical properties
explanation: Intermolecular forces are the attractive (and, at very short range, repulsive) forces that act between the particles — atoms, molecules, or ions — that make up a substance, distinct from the much stronger forces that hold the atoms within a single molecule together (intramolecular, or chemical bonding, forces). The strength of the intermolecular forces in a substance strongly influences many of its physical properties: substances with strong intermolecular forces tend to have particles held tightly together, giving them relatively high melting and boiling points (since more energy is needed to overcome these forces and allow particles to move freely, as covered in Heating Curves and Latent Heat), and are more likely to exist as solids or liquids at everyday, room temperature; substances with weak intermolecular forces have particles that are much more easily separated, giving them low melting and boiling points, and are more likely to exist as gases at room temperature. Intermolecular forces are also directly responsible for the different properties of the three states of matter, as covered in States of Matter, with the forces being strongest (relative to particle motion) in a solid, intermediate in a liquid, and weakest (or negligible) in a gas.
key_concepts: Forces between particles (distinct from stronger intramolecular/bonding forces)
Strength relates to melting/boiling point and state at room temperature
Strongest in solids, intermediate in liquids, weakest/negligible in gases

definitions.definition: The attractive (and, at short range, repulsive) forces acting between the particles of a substance, distinct from the stronger forces holding atoms together within a single molecule.

worked_examples.problem: Substance A has a much higher boiling point than substance B. Explain what this suggests about the relative strength of the intermolecular forces in each substance.
steps: Boiling requires overcoming the intermolecular forces holding the liquid's particles together closely enough to escape into the gas state.
A higher boiling point means more energy must be supplied to achieve this separation.

Since substance A requires more energy (a higher temperature/boiling point) to separate its particles than substance B does, this suggests that substance A has stronger intermolecular forces than substance B.
worked_examples.answer: Substance A likely has stronger intermolecular forces than substance B, since more energy (reflected in its higher boiling point) is needed to overcome these forces and separate its particles into a gas.

practical_applications: Predicting and explaining the melting and boiling points of different substances in chemistry and materials science
Designing materials with specific desired physical properties (e.g. adhesives, lubricants) based on intermolecular force strength
Understanding surface tension and viscosity, both influenced by the strength of intermolecular forces in a liquid
common_mistakes: Confusing intermolecular forces (between separate particles) with intramolecular (chemical bonding) forces (within a single molecule), which are typically much stronger
Assuming all substances have the same strength of intermolecular forces, ignoring the significant variation that determines different melting/boiling points
misconceptions: That intermolecular forces and the chemical bonds holding a molecule together are the same thing, or comparable in strength — intermolecular forces (acting between separate molecules) are generally very significantly weaker than the intramolecular (chemical bonding) forces holding the atoms within a single molecule together, which is why substances can melt or boil (overcoming intermolecular forces) without breaking apart their individual molecules (which would require overcoming the much stronger intramolecular forces).
tips: Remember 'inter-' means 'between' (intermolecular = between different molecules) while 'intra-' means 'within' (intramolecular = within a single molecule) — this distinction is key to understanding why melting a substance does not usually break its individual molecules apart.

basic: State whether intermolecular forces are generally stronger or weaker than intramolecular (chemical bonding) forces.
intermediate: Explain why a substance with weak intermolecular forces is likely to exist as a gas at room temperature.
advanced: Explain, using intermolecular forces, why a solid generally requires more energy to melt than the same substance requires to be heated further as a liquid to a similar temperature increase.

exam_questions: Explain how the relative strength of intermolecular forces in a substance affects its melting and boiling points.

basic: Generally weaker.
intermediate: Weak intermolecular forces mean the particles of the substance are only weakly attracted to each other, requiring very little energy to overcome these forces and allow the particles to move far apart and freely, which is exactly the particle behaviour of a gas; this is why substances with weak intermolecular forces are typically already gases at normal room temperature, since only a small amount of thermal energy (already present at room temperature) is needed to keep the particles separated.
advanced: Melting a solid requires overcoming a significant portion of the intermolecular forces holding particles in their fixed lattice positions, which typically requires a substantial input of energy (latent heat) without necessarily increasing temperature; heating a liquid further (without changing state) instead increases the average kinetic energy (and therefore the temperature) of particles that are already free to move, requiring comparatively less energy input for the same temperature change, since it does not need to overcome the additional structural forces holding a solid's fixed arrangement together.
exam: Stronger intermolecular forces hold a substance's particles together more tightly, requiring more energy (and therefore a higher temperature) to overcome these forces during melting or boiling, resulting in higher melting and boiling points; conversely, weaker intermolecular forces require less energy to overcome, resulting in lower melting and boiling points, and substances with sufficiently weak intermolecular forces may already be liquids or gases at typical room temperature.

summary: Intermolecular forces are the attractive forces between a substance's particles, distinct from the stronger intramolecular (bonding) forces within a molecule. Their strength determines melting and boiling points and the substance's state at room temperature, being strongest in solids and weakest in gases.
revision_notes: Forces BETWEEN particles (distinct from stronger bonding forces WITHIN a molecule)
Stronger forces = higher melting/boiling point
Strongest in solids, weakest/negligible in gases
